intro.title: Explore Parque Natural Cerro Verde
intro.description: Parque Natural Cerro Verde is located in the Santa Ana Department of El Salvador, 77 kilometers from the capital, San Salvador. It is a beautiful national park situated on an extinct volcano. Featuring spectacular volcanic landscapes and a rich cloud forest ecosystem, it is one of El Salvador's most important nature reserves and ecotourism destinations.

visitGuide.title: Visiting Tips
items: Park is open Monday to Sunday 08:00–20:00
Comfortable hiking or walking shoes are recommended
Bring a camera to capture the spectacular panoramas of Izalco and Santa Ana volcanoes
Carry enough water, insect repellent, and sunscreen

alsoKnownAs.title: Highlights
items: Spectacular Volcanic Landscapes: Features excellent viewpoints for perfect panoramas of Izalco Volcano, Santa Ana Volcano, and Lake Coatepeque.
Rich Cloud Forest Ecosystem: Home to a variety of endemic flora and fauna (like various orchids and birds), a paradise for nature lovers.
Cool Climate: At an altitude of about 2030 meters, the climate is pleasantly cool year-round.
Prime Location: Located in the Santa Ana Department with convenient access, serving as the heart of the 'Volcano Complex'.

route.title: Tour Route
route.overview: The ideal route to explore Parque Natural Cerro Verde:
steps: Start at the entrance and walk through the dense cloud forest trails.
Stop at the main viewpoints to capture stunning panoramic photos.
Join a guided hiking tour of the surrounding areas.
Rest in the park's picnic area and enjoy the peace of nature.
supplements: It's recommended to go in the morning when there's less cloud cover and highest visibility, offering a clearer view of the volcanoes.
Pay attention to sun protection and warmth, as UV rays are strong and temperatures are lower at high altitudes.
Please take your trash with you to protect the natural ecological environment.

transport.selfDriveDesc: Located in the Santa Ana Department, 77 km from San Salvador. It is highly recommended to drive or rent a car using navigation. The roads are good, and there is a dedicated paid parking lot at the top.
transport.busDesc: Long-distance buses to the park are available from Santa Ana or Sonsonate, but pay attention to the schedule.

transport.tipsDesc: Parque Natural Cerro Verde is an excellent place to experience El Salvador's natural beauty and a top choice for family trips. Visiting during sunny daylight hours is recommended.

officialManagement.title: About Parque Natural Cerro Verde
officialManagement.text: Parque Natural Cerro Verde is a famous natural attraction in the Santa Ana Department, boasting spectacular mountain views and rich natural and cultural value. It is directly managed and maintained by the Salvadoran Institute of Tourism (ISTU).

historyTimeline.title: History & Significance of Parque Natural Cerro Verde

items.title: Early Period: Natural Formation
items.description: Cerro Verde is an ancient extinct volcano that has evolved over time into a lush cloud forest, long regarded as a natural sacred site by local indigenous people.

items.title: 20th Century: Tourism Development
items.description: With the development of tourism in El Salvador, Cerro Verde gradually built viewpoints and trails, becoming the best and safest location to view neighboring active volcanoes.

items.title: 21st Century: Ecotourism Destination
items.description: In the 21st century, with its excellent facilities and spectacular natural scenery, it has attracted tourists worldwide and become an important calling card for El Salvador's ecotourism.

historyTimeline.guideContent: When visiting, you can start by strolling along the nature trails from the entrance; then stop at various viewpoints to admire the breathtaking twin volcanoes and lake views; if you have enough stamina and time, this is also the starting point for climbing the Santa Ana and Izalco volcanoes. Finally, enjoy local food or coffee in the park's rest area and feel the tranquility of nature.

weather.title: Live Weather & 7-Day Forecast
weather.subtitle: The park sits on a volcanic plateau around 2,030 m above sea level, where weather changes faster than in the city: afternoon showers are common and the summit is windy and cool. Check today and the next 7 days before you set off.
weather.unavailable: Live weather is temporarily unavailable. Please refresh the page shortly.
weather.neutral: Conditions look calm today — nothing special to flag. As always on the summit, pack a light jacket for the wind and sunscreen for the strong altitude sun.

adv.pSunny: Clear skies are ideal for the volcano panorama: visibility is at its best in the early morning for Izalco Volcano, Santa Ana Volcano and Lake Coatepeque.
adv.pOvercast: Overcast light is soft and glare-free, great for a long cloud-forest walk; trails stay damp, so watch your footing.
adv.oPrecip: Rain chance around {p}%: take some rain gear with you — it packs small.
adv.pPrecip: Mountain showers usually arrive after noon: do the main cloud-forest trails in the morning and keep the afternoon flexible.
adv.gPrecip: Compact umbrella or light rain jacket (a jacket suits the summit wind better)
adv.oDrizzle: Light rain or drizzle: with mountain winds an umbrella is awkward — a waterproof jacket works better.
adv.pDrizzle: Wet boardwalks get slippery — slow down in grippy shoes; the misty forest has its own quiet charm.
adv.gDrizzle: Light rain jacket or compact umbrella
adv.pThunder: Thunderstorms: leave the crater rim, open viewpoints and tall trees at once; shelter in your vehicle or a park building.
adv.pHvyRain: Heavy rain: stay on main trails and avoid steep valleys or poorly drained spots; if sections of trail close, follow the on-site guidance.
adv.gHvyRain: Waterproof jacket (and rain trousers); skip the long umbrella — summit winds will turn it inside out
adv.pFog: Morning cloud is common: if volcano views are your goal, wait until after about 9 a.m., when the mist usually lifts.
adv.pWindMid: Windy: gusts are strongest at the crater and viewpoints — don't linger in exposed spots and hold gear steady when shooting.
adv.gWindMid: A hat with a chin strap; avoid loose, flappy clothing
adv.oHeat: It turns warm around midday: light, breathable quick-dry layers beat heavy clothing.
adv.pHeat: Avoid 11:00–14:00 in the hottest, most exposed areas; save hiking for early morning or late afternoon.
adv.gHeat: Plenty of drinking water; electrolytes or heat-protection items are a bonus
adv.pUv: UV is very strong: limit time in open sun around noon and reapply sunscreen every 2 hours.
adv.gUv: Sunscreen, wide-brim hat and sunglasses (UV is strong at altitude — even on overcast days)
adv.oDiff: Temperatures swing about {diff}°C between night and day: a light layer for dawn and dusk.
adv.oLowMax: High of only about {max}°C today — dress warm: a thick jacket or fleece.
adv.gLowMax: Warm hat, scarf and hot drinks
adv.oCoolNow: It is about {now}°C right now: a long-sleeve plus a light jacket fits the bill; shed layers as it warms up.
adv.rThunder: Lightning safety: during a storm stay off the crater rim, summit and open viewpoints; move to your vehicle or a park building.
adv.rHeavyRain: Heavy rain: trails turn slick and valleys can flood; sections of trail may close temporarily — follow on-site notices.
adv.rWind: Strong wind: gusts at the crater and cliff viewpoints are intense — stay back from the edge, hold the railing and avoid dead trees or temporary structures.
adv.rFog: Thick fog or low cloud: visibility is poor and volcano views may be hidden — stay on the main trails and never wander off route.
adv.rSnow: Cold precipitation (snow or freezing rain): icy surfaces are likely — dress warmly and check trail or park notices.
adv.pSnow: Snow or freezing rain makes trails cold and slippery: skip hiking, wait in the visitor area and watch for park updates.

services.title: Visitor Services & Nearby Facilities
services.subtitle: Practical information organised by type of service — neutral and vendor-neutral, with no specific business recommendations.
services.note: Note: the park is mountainous with fairly limited facilities; bring water and snacks before you arrive. Always confirm what is available on site.

items.name: Restrooms & park service point
items.description: Restrooms and a visitor service point stand at the entrance — the last place to ask questions and stock up before you set out.

items.name: Parking
items.description: The main lot charges by vehicle type. Spaces fill quickly at weekends and holidays, so arriving early helps.

items.name: Food & drinks
items.description: Light meals, snacks and coffee are available in and around the park for a post-visit break; bringing your own snacks and water is the safest bet.

items.name: Accommodation
items.description: The park and its surroundings offer mountain lodges and campsites; for more services head to the towns in the valley and confirm they are open before booking.

items.name: Shops & supermarkets
items.description: Towns below the mountain have supermarkets and convenience stores — buy snacks and water before driving up.

items.name: Fuel & EV charging
items.description: The access road is a mountain road: fill up in the valley first. EV drivers should confirm charging types and the nearest stations in advance.

items.name: Medical & emergency
items.description: Mountain medical resources are limited — bring your own medication and call local emergency numbers in case of need.

seasons.title: Seasonal Visiting Guide
seasons.subtitle: A look at long-term climate patterns across weather, nature and experience to help you choose the right time to visit.

rows.title: Dry season
rows.weather: Mostly clear, little rain and high visibility; strong summit sun by day and noticeably cool mornings and evenings.
rows.nature: The cloud forest is at its driest and viewpoints are at their clearest — volcano panoramas and the lake in full view.
rows.advice: The best season overall. Cloud cover is thinnest from 8–9 a.m.; plan hiking and viewpoints for the morning.

rows.title: Rainy season
rows.weather: A rhythm of clear mornings and afternoon showers; humid air and mostly short-lived rain.
rows.nature: Vegetation and orchids are at their most lush, waterfalls run full and birds are active — greenest time of year.
rows.advice: Go in the morning and carry a waterproof jacket; shelter in the visitor area or a building when a shower passes.

seasons.note: These are long-term averages. For a single day, check the live weather and 7-day forecast at the top of this page.

personas.title: Plans Tailored to How You Travel
personas.subtitle: Whether you visit with kids, for photography, or at an easy pace, the cloud forest can be matched to your rhythm.

items.name: Family & Kids, Easy
items.summary: Viewpoints, a short cloud-forest loop and a picnic — a relaxed pace that leaves time for kids to watch orchids, birds and butterflies.
points: Start at the main viewpoint: kids love Izalco Volcano's perfect cone
Walk the short cloud-forest loop (about 40 min); hold hands on damp trails
Bring snacks and plenty of water; refill at the picnic area
Grippy shoes and sun-protective long sleeves for kids, plus a light jacket for the wind

items.name: Photography & Nature
items.summary: Morning seas of cloud, afternoon light between the trees, orchids and hummingbirds — give it time and the forest rewards you.
points: 6–9 a.m. is the best window for cloud seas and soft light — claim your spot early
Telephoto for volcanoes and birds; macro for orchids and dew
Summit winds are constant: use a sturdy tripod and keep lens hoods secure
Overcast light is actually great for the forest interior — don't wait only for blue skies

items.name: Easy Pace & Accessibility
items.summary: The main parking area sits close to the key viewpoints, so a little walking brings open views; the park is still mountain terrain with slopes on some trails — go at your own pace.
points: Park in the main lot and take the shortest route to the viewpoints
Bring a seat or walking pole and rest often
For wheelchairs or walkers, contact the visitor point in advance to confirm accessible sections
Mornings and wet days are cooler — dress warmly and watch for slippery ground

itinerary.title: Recommended Self-Guided Routes
itinerary.subtitle: Two tried-and-tested general routes — one for a limited schedule, one for a deeper visit.

plans.title: Half-Day Highlights
plans.summary: Focus on the best of it: a short cloud-forest loop, the main viewpoint panorama and a scenic picnic — no rush.
steps: Arrive before 8:00 a.m. (easier parking, thinnest morning cloud)
Warm up on the short cloud-forest trail (about 40 minutes)
Enjoy the panorama of Izalco, Santa Ana and Lake Coatepeque from the main viewpoint (about 40 minutes)
Recharge at the picnic area or a coffee spot
Take a last look from the viewpoint near the exit, gather your things and head back

plans.title: Full-Day Deep Route
plans.summary: If your fitness allows, join a guided climb of Santa Ana or Izalco Volcano with Cerro Verde as your base.
steps: Arrive at 7:30 and confirm guide meet-up time and gear requirements
Climb the neighbouring volcano with your guide (about 4–6 hours round trip, including summit time)
Lunch and rest after descending; refill water
Return to Cerro Verde for a short trail or viewpoint time as the light changes
Wrap up before sunset and allow time for the drive back

tips: At altitude, walk slowly and drink water in small sips often
Dry-season mornings can drop to 10–12°C — bring layers
In the rainy season, hike in the morning and keep afternoons flexible
Stay on officially open trails and off the vegetation
Volcano climbs must be led by a licensed guide — never go alone

science.title: Cloud Forest Science & Visitor Responsibility
science.subtitle: Understand the cloud forest before you go, and every footstep gets a little lighter.

topics.title: Where the clouds come from
topics.body: Moist Pacific air is pushed up the mountain, cools and condenses into the clouds that wrap the summit for much of the year — that is where the cloud forest gets its name. The damp feeds mosses, ferns and orchids on every trunk and keeps the forest floor soft and humid.

topics.title: A forest that grew on a dead volcano
topics.body: Cerro Verde is a long-dormant volcano; over millions of years weathering built soil and the slopes turned to forest. Neighbouring Santa Ana Volcano is still active — together they form a natural classroom for the life cycle of volcanoes.

topics.title: An oasis on a migration corridor
topics.body: Central America is a key corridor for species moving between the Americas, and cloud forests act as oases along the way: orchids, bromeliads, hummingbirds and migratory birds all depend on these wet mountain woodlands.

duties: Walk only on officially open trails and never into the vegetation
Do not pick orchids or plants; do not disturb or feed wildlife
Take all your rubbish with you — leave no trace
Do not climb over barriers at the crater rim or cliff viewpoints
During thunderstorms or high winds, follow park instructions and leave promptly
science.note: Carry the beauty home in your memory — and leave only footprints on the trail.

stories.title: The Name of the Green Mountain: A Valley Legend
stories.text: Cerro Verde means “Green Mountain.” In stories passed down through generations here, the dormant volcano forever wrapped in cloud and green is remembered as a guardian watching over Lake Coatepeque and the volcanic plain below. When Izalco growled in the night and lit the sky, people would look to Cerro Verde — still quietly wearing its green — a reminder that this land, restless as it can be, is also rich and worth protecting. Today it is a national park, where orchids, pines and endless birdsong continue to grow, carrying that legendary “guardian green” into real conservation.

seo.aboutTitle: About Parque Natural Cerro Verde (Santa Ana)
seo.aboutLead: Welcome to **Parque Natural Cerro Verde**, widely recognized as the **Cerro Verde** national park destination. Located in the heart of **Santa Ana**, **Santa Ana Department**, **El Salvador**, this destination serves as a primary hub for travelers visiting the region. The park stands on an extinct volcano at about 2,030 metres, protecting a lush cloud forest and offering panoramic viewpoints over Izalco Volcano, Santa Ana Volcano and Lake Coatepeque.
seo.nearbySubtitle: Points of interest reachable from Parque Natural Cerro Verde
seo.nearbyIntro: When visiting **Parque Natural Cerro Verde**, visitors can easily explore surrounding natural landmarks and points of interest, including **Santa Ana Volcano** and **Izalco Volcano**.

nearby.name: Santa Ana Volcano (Volcán Ilamatepec)
nearby.description: El Salvador's tallest volcano (2,381 m) and the park's next-door neighbour. From Cerro Verde you can join a guided hike up to its crater, one of the country's most rewarding volcano experiences.

nearby.name: Izalco Volcano (Volcán de Izalco)
nearby.description: A young, near-perfect cone nicknamed the 'Lighthouse of the Pacific'. The viewpoints inside the park offer some of the best panoramas of its iconic silhouette.

nearby.name: Lake Coatepeque (Lago de Coatepeque)
nearby.description: A vast volcanic crater lake just a short drive from the park, ideal for swimming, boating and relaxing after a morning exploring Cerro Verde.

seo.faqSubtitle: Everything you need to know before visiting Parque Natural Cerro Verde

faq.q: Where is Parque Natural Cerro Verde located?
faq.a: Parque Natural Cerro Verde is located in Santa Ana Department, El Salvador, about 77 km from San Salvador. The Google Maps plus code is R9GG+84V, Santa Ana, El Salvador.

faq.q: Is Cerro Verde free to visit?
faq.a: No, Parque Natural Cerro Verde charges an entrance fee set by the Salvadoran Institute of Tourism (ISTU): US$1.50 for nationals and US$3.00 for foreigners. Parking costs US$1.00 for light vehicles and US$2.00 for heavy vehicles. Fees may change, so please check the official announcement before your visit.

faq.q: What is the best time to visit Parque Natural Cerro Verde?
faq.a: The best time is the dry season (November to April), especially in the morning when the sky is clearest and you can see Izalco Volcano, Santa Ana Volcano and Lake Coatepeque in full view.

faq.q: Do I need a guide to climb the volcanoes from Cerro Verde?
faq.a: Yes, guided hikes are required to climb nearby volcanoes such as Santa Ana Volcano and Izalco Volcano. Guides can be arranged at the park, and a tip is appreciated.

faq.q: How do I get to Parque Natural Cerro Verde from San Salvador?
faq.a: The park is about 77 km from San Salvador. Most visitors drive or hire a car and follow navigation to Parque Natural Cerro Verde. Public buses from Santa Ana or Sonsonate also serve the area.

faq.q: How long should I spend at Parque Natural Cerro Verde?
faq.a: Half a day is enough to walk the cloud forest trails and enjoy the viewpoints. Allow a full day if you also plan a guided ascent of Santa Ana Volcano or Izalco Volcano.
